method: Agent-authored manual reading against each complete source answer; not independent human review. Exact full answers are retained as support excerpts. No model predictions informed selection or wording.

checks.point: Faithfulness checks claims against retrieved context.
answerExcerpts: The RAG Triad checks three links. Faithfulness, or groundedness, asks whether each claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved context, and this is the direct check for hallucination. Context relevance asks whether the retrieved passages are relevant to the question, which tests the retriever. Answer relevance asks whether the answer actually addresses the question. Scoring all three separately tells you whether a failure came from retrieval or from generation.

checks.point: Citation precision measures whether cited passages support adjacent claims.
answerExcerpts: Three genuinely separate metrics, because they catch three different failure modes: citation precision (of the passages actually cited, what fraction genuinely support the claim next to them — measured via NLI entailment between the cited passage and the specific claim); citation recall (of the claims the response makes, what fraction have any citation at all — requires segmenting the response into atomic claims first); and attribution accuracy (does the cited passage actually say what the response claims it says, which is distinct from hallucination detection, since hallucination checks if *any* passage supports a claim, while attribution accuracy checks specifically whether *the cited one* does).

checks.point: Block deployments on golden-set regressions beyond threshold.
answerExcerpts: Four layers, and naming all four (in order) is what separates a senior answer from "we have an eval set": a pre-deploy CI gate running the golden-dataset eval that blocks the deploy on any metric regression beyond threshold; a canary rollout to a small traffic slice, comparing guardrail metrics (latency, error rate, refusal rate) and judge scores canary-vs-control before full rollout; post-rollout online signals (regeneration rate, rephrase rate, thumbs ratio, escalation rate) watched against a pre-deploy baseline window; and trace-level triage when any signal fires — pulling the actual failing traces, localizing which stage broke using per-stage scores, and promoting those failures into the golden set so the exact same regression gets caught pre-deploy the next time around.

checks.point: Pass at one measures first-sample task success.
answerExcerpts: Pass at one says the first sample fixes the task on about six tasks in ten. Pass at five says that at least one of five samples passes on almost every task, so the right answer is usually within reach and the gap is selection. Report both, with the raw pass counts per task, because pass at k alone hides an agent that succeeds once in twenty tries.

checks.point: ECE averages confidence-accuracy gaps across weighted bins.
answerExcerpts: ECE bins predictions by confidence and averages the gap between confidence and accuracy, weighted by bin size. With ten bins and a hundred predictions you cannot tell 0.02 from noise, and inside one bin overconfident and underconfident predictions can offset each other in the bin average. Add the Brier score, the mean squared error between confidence and outcome per prediction, and report how many bins were populated.

checks.point: Keep rules reachable within two hops of the router.
answerExcerpts: There are three independent causes, and any one of them is enough. The rule is three hops from the router, past the two-hop reachability limit, so the agent never loads it, and it is prose with no check, so nothing refuses the write even when the agent reads it. And the root file conflicts with the database document, and conflicting instructions silently move an agent from asking to guessing. Fix the reach first, make the rule an approval-category rule with a block-severity check, and remove the conflict.

checks.point: ReAct cycles through thought, action and observation.
answerExcerpts: A ReAct agent repeats a cycle of thought, action, and observation. The model reasons about what to do, calls a tool, reads the result, and continues until it can answer. Tools are defined with clear schemas, and their calls are parsed and validated before they run. To prevent runaway loops, enforce a maximum number of steps, plus time and cost budgets. Also detect repeated identical calls and break the cycle, then stop gracefully or hand off to a person.

checks.point: Five apps and twenty tools require 100 bespoke integrations.
answerExcerpts:
5 × 20 = 100 separate integrations. With MCP, each app implements a client once and each tool a server once: 5 + 20 = 25. That N × M to N + M change is the problem MCP solves.

A standardized protocol for connecting an AI application to external tools/data sources, so one client implementation works against any MCP-compatible server instead of every app needing bespoke integration code per tool.

checks.point: A handoff needs summary, changed files and commands.
answerExcerpts: The paragraph is a status report, and a handoff needs seven fields: a summary, the changed files, the commands run, the failed attempts, the open risks, the next action and a pointer to the verification and review reports. The next action is the most important field, because it makes the first step of the next session deterministic. Generate the packet from the workbench artifacts instead of asking the agent to write it, and run a cleanup check first so that the packet describes a tree the next session can trust.

checks.point: Inspect repeated action-observation pairs in the trace.
answerExcerpts: Read the trace for the pair of action and observation that repeats, then ask why the model does not react to the observation. The usual causes are an error that the loop never shows to the model, an observation that reads the same on every turn, and a missing turn budget. Fix the cause, then add the two guards that stop any future loop: a budget that yields control to the caller, and a check for a repeated action with a repeated observation.

checks.point: Measure TTFT and output-token time separately using percentiles.
answerExcerpts: Time to first token mostly reflects queueing plus the prefill phase that processes the prompt. Time per output token reflects the decode phase, which generates tokens one at a time. Measure them separately, using percentiles and not just averages. To reduce time to first token, shorten prompts and use prompt caching so a shared prefix reuses its KV cache. To reduce time per output token, use efficient batching, quantization, or a smaller model. Streaming tokens as they are generated also makes the response feel faster.

checks.point: Store both key and value tensors per KV head.
answerExcerpts: Each layer stores a key and a value for each KV head: 2 × 32 layers × 8 heads × 128 dims × 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB per token. With full multi-head attention (32 KV heads) it would be 512 KiB. Grouped-query attention cuts the cache by 4× here.

checks.point: Repeated identical prefix prefill wastes compute.
answerExcerpts: Prefill for 3,000 identical tokens on every request is pure waste. Prefix caching stores the KV blocks for a common prefix and maps new requests onto them, cutting TTFT and compute. Many API providers bill cached input tokens at a discount for the same reason. Put the stable parts of the prompt first and the variable parts last, so the shared prefix stays as long as possible.

checks.point: Batch-dependent floating-point reductions can change top logits.
answerExcerpts: The batch changed the arithmetic. Floating-point addition is not associative, and the kernels split their sums by the batch size, so the same request adds its numbers in a different order in a batch of 3 than in a batch of 30; a change in the last bit can flip the top logit, and every later token then follows a different text. The prefix cache does the same, because a request that reuses cached blocks runs a different prefill path, and so does the dtype. A seed fixes only the random draws of sampling, so it is not enough: offline, run the engine in one process with the same order; online, use the batch-invariant mode and pay its speed cost.

checks.point: Use data-parallel replicas when model and cache fit on one GPU.
answerExcerpts: Ask three questions. If the model fits on one GPU with room for the KV cache you need, use data parallelism, one full copy per GPU, and the output grows with the copies. If it does not fit, split it: tensor parallelism inside one machine when the GPUs have a fast link and the GPU count divides the attention heads, and pipeline parallelism when they do not or when the model needs more than one machine. Tensor parallelism talks after every layer, pipeline parallelism once per stage boundary, and data parallelism not at all between copies.

checks.point: Weight-only quantization compresses stored parameters.
answerExcerpts: Weight-only quantization compresses just the stored weights, which reduces size and memory with a simple process, and is common for GPU serving. Weight-activation quantization also quantizes activations at runtime. It can reduce computation further, but activations contain outliers that hurt accuracy if they are quantized naively. Methods such as SmoothQuant and AWQ handle this by protecting the salient weights and channels. Smaller models also need less memory bandwidth, which speeds up inference, so always measure accuracy against your speed gain.

Methods such as SmoothQuant and AWQ handle this by protecting the salient weights and channels. Smaller models also need less memory bandwidth, which speeds up inference, so always measure accuracy against your speed gain.

checks.point: Weight quantization does not shrink the separate KV budget.
answerExcerpts: The KV cache. Weight quantization shrinks the weights, and the cache for the running requests is a separate budget that stays in BF16 or FP8 and grows with every token in flight; at 128 concurrent requests with a 2k context the lesson puts it near 20 GB for a 70B model, plus about 5 GB of activations, so the total is about 60 GB on the 80 GB card. That 20 GB is the lesson's rough figure, so check it against the config: Llama-3.1-70B keeps 320 KiB per token in BF16, and 128 full 2k-token requests then need about four times the lesson's figure, which does not fit beside the weights on one 80 GB card. Count the weights, the cache at your peak concurrency and context, and the activations together, and read the pool size in the startup log after the start.

checks.point: FP8 weights free memory that can enlarge the KV pool.
answerExcerpts: Two effects multiply. The FP8 weights fell to 29.75 GB and freed 28.00 GB, which the fraction handed to the pool, so the pool grew from 20.80 GB to 49.58 GB in the units of the log; and each token took half the bytes, 49,152 instead of 98,304 for 48 layers with 4 KV heads of size 128. checks.point: Constrained decoding masks tokens that violate a schema.
answerExcerpts: The strongest guarantee is constrained decoding, where a grammar or JSON schema masks any token that would make the output invalid. You define the expected structure with a schema, for example using Pydantic, and pass it to the model. If validation fails, retry automatically with the error message, with a limit on the number of retries.

checks.point: Distinguish parse errors, schema violations and refusals.

Strict enforcement removes the first two by construction for a response that finishes. The refusal stays, and it must be a typed outcome that the code logs and returns, never a retry. A response cut at the token limit can still fail to parse, so check the stop reason before you read the output.

checks.point: Concurrent misses can duplicate expensive recomputation.
answerExcerpts: A popular cache entry expires (or the cache is cold after a restart), and many concurrent requests for that same key all miss simultaneously, each independently re-running the expensive underlying operation — generation, re-embedding, retrieval — wasting compute and potentially overwhelming the backend all at once. Standard preventions: request coalescing/single-flight (only the first miss actually recomputes; concurrent requests for the same key wait on that result instead of duplicating the work), a lock around the recompute-and-write step so only one caller repopulates the entry, probabilistic early expiration (recompute slightly before the real TTL, with increasing probability as expiry nears, to spread refreshes out instead of letting them all cliff-edge together), and proactive cache warming ahead of a known traffic spike or right after a deploy/restart.

checks.point: Treat external text as untrusted data.

Separate it from system instructions with clear delimiters, and remember that this reduces risk but does not eliminate it. checks.point: Resolve tenant identity and per-chunk permission metadata.
answerExcerpts: Seven steps, in order: clarify requirements first (single org or multi-tenant, how fresh must permission checks be — minutes or seconds, what scale of users/groups); ingestion via a connector that produces chunks plus embeddings plus resolved per-chunk ACL metadata; identity resolution where the user's group memberships get expanded at query time and cached with a short TTL; retrieval that pre-filters *inside* the ANN search itself on tenant and permission match, not after; a late-binding permission re-check against the authoritative source on the final top-k right before generation, failing closed on any gap; permission-awareness extended beyond retrieval itself (ACL-aware citations, permission-scoped cache keys, a zero-retention LLM endpoint); and an audit layer logging user, applied filter, and chunk IDs per query, plus periodic cross-tenant probe tests. Naming the two-gate model explicitly — a cheap metadata pre-filter plus an authoritative late-binding check — and the staleness window between them is what distinguishes a senior answer from "just add a metadata filter."

checks.point: Cross-tenant answer reuse can leak cached content.
answerExcerpts: Beyond a naive cross-tenant leak (Tenant A's cached answer served to Tenant B's semantically-similar query), there are two subtler ones: a timing side-channel, where a cache hit (fast) versus a cache miss (slow) lets one tenant infer whether another tenant has previously queried a given topic, purely from response latency; and document-ID leakage in cache metadata, where an implementation that caches retrieved chunk IDs alongside the answer exposes *which documents are relevant to a topic* even if the answer text itself is withheld. The fix for all three is the same: namespace every cache key by tenant/user ID and include a hash of the current permission set in the key, not just the query embedding.

checks.point: Classify toxicity, personal data and instruction leakage.
answerExcerpts: Put three classifiers on the model output behind one router: toxicity by rules, personal data by regexes for emails, phone numbers and card shaped strings, and instruction leakage by trigram overlap with the known system prompt. Each returns a severity, and the router takes the maximum and applies one action: block on high, redact on medium, warn on low, log on none. Run the classifiers in parallel with token streaming and hold the final chunk until the verdict arrives. Earlier chunks have already shipped, so where a block or a redaction must cover the whole response, hold the full response and accept the latency.

checks.point: Route using the maximum returned severity.

Each returns a severity, and the router takes the maximum and applies one action: block on high, redact on medium, warn on low, log on none. Run the classifiers in parallel with token streaming and hold the final chunk until the verdict arrives. Earlier chunks have already shipped, so where a block or a redaction must cover the whole response, hold the full response and accept the latency.
